questions.q: What is the standard form of a quadratic program (QP)?
options: minimize cᵀx subject to Ax ≤ b
minimize ½xᵀQx + cᵀx subject to Ax ≤ b, Ex = e
maximize xᵀx subject to no constraints
minimize ‖x‖ subject to Qx = 0
questions.explain: A QP minimizes a quadratic objective ½xᵀQx + cᵀx subject to linear inequality and equality constraints.

questions.q: Adding a no-short-selling constraint (w ≥ 0) to the minimum-variance problem does what to its solvability?
options: It has no effect; the closed-form Lagrangian solution still applies directly
It makes the problem non-convex and unsolvable
It keeps the problem convex but removes the closed-form algebraic solution, since the active set of binding constraints isn't known in advance
It turns the problem into a linear program automatically
questions.explain: The problem remains a convex QP (still guaranteed a global optimum), but because it's unknown in advance which weights will be pinned at zero, the simple Lagrangian equality-constraint algebra no longer applies directly, and a numerical QP solver is needed.

questions.q: What distinguishes a linear program (LP) from a quadratic program (QP)?
options: An LP has a linear objective and linear constraints, with no quadratic term in the objective
An LP must always have a negative optimal value
An LP never has inequality constraints
An LP and a QP are the same thing
questions.explain: A linear program minimizes a purely linear objective cᵀx subject to linear constraints, with no quadratic term, unlike a QP's ½xᵀQx + cᵀx objective.

questions.q: What does the 'active set' refer to in a constrained optimization problem with inequality constraints?
options: The set of all possible portfolios
The subset of inequality constraints that are exactly binding (tight) at the optimal solution
The set of assets with positive expected return
The eigenvalues of the covariance matrix
questions.explain: The active set is the subset of inequality constraints that hold with equality at the optimum (e.g., which portfolio weights are pinned exactly at their lower bound of zero).

questions.q: Why can scipy.optimize.linprog reliably find the true global optimum of a linear program?
options: Because LPs have a random objective function
Because linear programs are convex, so any locally optimal vertex found by simplex or interior-point methods is globally optimal
Because linprog ignores all constraints
Because LPs never have more than one variable
questions.explain: Linear programs are convex optimization problems, so the simplex and interior-point methods underlying linprog (e.g., the 'highs' method) are guaranteed to find the global optimum, not just a local one.
